profile.jobTitle: AI Inference Tools Software Engineer Intern
profile.summary:
As a computer science student at Brown University, I am passionate about exploring the intersection of technology and human connection. I am pursuing a concurrent bachelor's and master's degree in computer science, with a focus on machine learning and its applications in social media, healthcare, and wellness.

I have gained valuable research and development experience through various internships and projects. Most recently, I worked as a research intern at UC Irvine, where I built a deep learning classification model for senior fall risk assessment using Bio-Clinical BERT on nurse’s notes. I was one of the seven interns selected out of 100+ applicants for the REU research program funded by the NSF, and I presented my work in multiple conferences. I also worked as a software intern at the SCU Frugal Innovation Lab, where I helped develop a game-based Wolof/English/French language learning app for schools in Senegal, using React to build a database interface website for teachers. Additionally, I participated in a fellowship at Headstream Innovation, where I designed and created my own project about the impact of social media on youth wellbeing, and shared my insights and resources by presenting at multiple conferences to social tech startups in the Headstream Accelerator and to the general public through an Instagram page and podcast.

I am always eager to learn new skills and technologies, and to collaborate with diverse and talented people. I have strong communication, data analysis, and activism skills, and I enjoy applying them to create positive social change. My goal is to leverage my knowledge and passion for machine learning, human connection, and wellness, to develop innovative and ethical solutions that can improve the lives of people and communities.

projects.title: Predicting Fall Risk Using Deep Learning on Nursing Notes
projects.description:
Falls are a primary source of injury and possible death for older adults, affecting 28% of people 65 and older (CDC 2020). Manual tools for fall risk assessment require clinician check-ups or human review of health records. Additionally, past research using predictive machine learning models relies on features from a specific hospital system’s health record format, which is not generalizable to other hospital systems. 

To build a fall risk prediction deep learning model, we fine-tuned Bio-Clinical BERT, a foundation large language model pre-trained on clinical data, to perform classification on nursing notes and predict high risk, moderate risk, or low risk. The nursing notes were from MIMIC-III, a database of de-identified health records associated with over 40,000 patients over an 11-year period. The notes were labeled as high, moderate, or low risk using a lexicon of fall-related terms created by clinician focus groups. Next, the notes were filtered by removing the sentences in each note containing mentions of fall-related terms. So, the model is trained to recognize correlations between other risk factors and fall risk level instead of specific mentions of falls.

The model reached 86% accuracy on testing data after around 6 hours. We used an Nvidia V100 GPU after running for 3 epochs using a batch size of 1024 and a learning rate of 1e-3. 

Automating fall risk assessment decreases the manual monitoring burden on medical professionals and provides a model that could be used to identify high-risk individuals to decrease the number of falls.
